opus-5.5.text:
I think first-party products like Claude Code and ChatGPT Agent are a very important signal of where the whole industry is going. In the early days, people thought of the model as a kind of engine, and products were built on top of it by other companies. That's still true to some extent, but what we're seeing now is that the model and the product are converging. When the model gets strong enough at agentic tasks, like writing code, using tools, browsing, and running long multi-step workflows, the boundary between "model capability" and "product experience" becomes very blurry.

Take Claude Code as an example. In a sense it's a fairly thin product. It's a terminal interface, a set of tools, and a loop. But it works extremely well because the model itself was trained to be good at exactly that kind of environment. The product and the training are co-designed. I think that's the key insight: whoever trains the model has a natural advantage in building the agent, because they can shape the model's behavior around the product's real usage, and the usage data flows back into training. It's a very tight feedback loop.

So I'd say the future of first-party agent products is quite bright, but it also changes the competitive landscape. For a model company, you can't just publish a model and an API and expect others to discover all the value. You need to understand at least a few high-value scenarios deeply yourself, because that's how you know what capabilities to push in training. Coding is the first one because it's verifiable, it has clear economic value, and the environment is relatively clean. General computer use and research-type agents will follow.

At the same time, I don't think this means third-party products disappear. There will be a lot of vertical scenarios where domain knowledge, distribution, and workflow integration matter a lot, and a model company can't do everything. But the horizontal, general-purpose agent layer, the thing that sits closest to the model's core capability, will increasingly be owned by the companies that train the models.

For us, the lesson is that model capability is still the foundation. If the model isn't good at agentic reasoning and long-horizon tasks, no amount of product polish will fix it. But once the model is good, you should put it into a real product as early as possible, let real users stress-test it, and let that shape the next round of training. I think that loop, between model, product, and data, is what really decides who wins in the agent era.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the rise of first-party products is actually one of the most important signals in the industry right now, and it tells us something about where the value is going to sit.

For a long time the assumption was that the model labs would be like infrastructure providers, and a layer of application companies on top would own the user. What Claude Code and ChatGPT Agent show is that this separation is not stable. When the capability itself is the product, the people who train the model have a structural advantage. They see the failure modes first, they can shape the training data toward the product, and they can close the loop between what users actually do and what the next model learns. That loop is very hard for a third party to replicate, because you are always working with a frozen snapshot.

So my first view is that agentic products will increasingly be built by the labs themselves, especially in the categories closest to the model's core strengths, like coding, research and general computer use. These are the areas where the product is almost a thin shell around the model, and the shell gets thinner every generation.

But I don't think this means there is no room for others. There are two spaces that remain open. One is domains where the data and the workflow are proprietary, where a lab cannot easily get the feedback signal. Finance, law, specific verticals of enterprise software. The other is form factor. The labs are optimizing for generality, and a focused team can still win on a specific interface or a specific context in which the agent lives.

From our side, the lesson we take is to not be a wrapper. If you are a model company, your product has to be something that makes your model better, not just something that sells it. The product is a data engine and an evaluation environment as much as it is a revenue line. I think the labs that understand this will compound, and the ones that treat products as distribution will fall behind.

The last thing I'd say is that the real competition in the next few years is probably not between agent products but between the underlying loops. Whoever can run the fastest cycle from user interaction to model improvement, at scale and with good taste about what to learn from, will end up owning the first-party agent category. That is a very different kind of race from the one we were in two years ago, which was mostly about benchmark scores.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much of the user’s work these products can actually complete. There’s a big difference between giving you a useful answer and carrying a task through to a result you can trust.

Coding is a good example because there’s a feedback loop: the system can make a change, run tests, and use the results to improve its next step. For a more general agent, the objective can be less clear, and success is harder to verify. So I would expect progress to be uneven across different kinds of work.

First-party products have an advantage because the model and the product can evolve together. You can discover a limitation in the user experience and address it through both training and product design. But that doesn’t mean model companies will own every application. Understanding a particular workflow, integrating with existing systems, and earning users’ trust still matter a lot.

Over time, I think the interaction shifts from asking questions to delegating tasks. The challenge is knowing when the agent can proceed independently and when it needs your input. Getting that balance right will be just as important as making the model more capable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think first-party AI products will increasingly move from answering questions to completing tasks. With something like Claude Code, the important shift is that the model can work inside an environment, make changes, and check whether those changes actually solve the problem. For a more general agent, the challenge is doing that reliably across a much wider range of tasks.

There’s also a strong feedback loop between the product and the model. When you build both, you can see where users get stuck and use those observations to guide model improvements. Better models then make new product experiences possible.

But I don’t think that means first-party products will capture everything. There’s still a lot of room for products built around specific workflows and customer needs. The key question is who can turn model capability into a dependable result. Users care about getting their work done, and the product has to deliver that consistently.
